title: Correct without shaming
hook: from Alexander the grammarian: correct people's mistakes by saying the right thing yourself (Meditations 1.10)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Sextus and his fatherly household. Your line was patient with the unlearned.

A four-year-old announces, I goed to the park. You have choices. You can say, no, it's went, say it again. Or you can say, you went to the park? What did you see? Most parents learn, sooner or later, that the second way works better, and nobody cries. Nearly two thousand years ago, a teacher of Greek grammar did the same with grown men, including a future emperor, and Marcus thought it worth a whole entry.
screen: `I GOED TO THE PARK.` → `YOU WENT? WHAT DID YOU SEE?` → `CORRECT WITHOUT SHAMING.`

segments.voice: First, the teacher. Alexander was a grammarian, a professional teacher of Greek language and literature, a respected job in Rome, and he taught the young Marcus. A grammarian's whole life is noticing mistakes. Second, what he didn't do. Marcus says he learned from Alexander not to find fault, and not to jump on people who used a clumsy word, a wrong form or an odd-sounding phrase. No pouncing. No public correction. Third, what he did instead. He would slip the right expression into the conversation himself, neatly: as part of his answer, or while agreeing with the person, or while talking with them about the real subject, the thing itself, not the word. The other person heard the right form, and nobody had been made small. Fourth, why it works. Corrected in front of others, people usually hear one thing: that they were wrong in public. The lesson vanishes under the embarrassment. Said right, in passing, the lesson arrives without the sting, and they can pick it up, or not. And notice Alexander's priority: the conversation stays on the subject, not the slip. This reaches past grammar. A friend mispronounces a name. A colleague gets a fact slightly wrong in a meeting. A parent uses an old word for something. Often the kindest correction is just the right word, said gently, in the next sentence. Marcus, who would one day have the power to humiliate anyone, wrote down a teacher who refused to.
screen: `ALEXANDER, A TEACHER OF GRAMMAR.` · `NO POUNCING ON MISTAKES.` · `SLIP THE RIGHT WORD IN YOURSELF.` · `KEEP TO THE THING, NOT THE SLIP.` · then, large: `SAY IT RIGHT, GENTLY.`

segments.voice: Remember a time someone corrected you in front of others, and feel how it landed, even now. Then replay a time you did it to someone else, without judging it, but this time just use the right word yourself, in passing, and keep talking about the real subject. Watch their face in this version.
Alexander. The grammarian who never pounced on a mistake, saying the right thing himself, in passing, and keeping to the subject. Today's word.
Your line: say it right, gently. Keep to the thing, not the slip. Day five hundred twenty-seven, done.

screen: `DAY 527 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FREE SPEECH AND EQUAL RIGHTS.`

howItsDone: Many parents, teachers and colleagues practice something like Alexander's way: they repeat the correct word or fact naturally in their reply instead of pointing out the mistake.

notes: Meditations 1.10 paraphrased: from Alexander the grammarian, to refrain from fault-finding and not to reproach those who uttered any barbarous or solecistic or strange-sounding expression, but dexterously to introduce the very expression which ought to have been used, by way of answer, or giving confirmation, or joining in an inquiry about the thing itself, not about the word.
